utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We apologise for our delay in starting, but we had information about the absence of Judge Nosworthy, which we had to reflect upon. We hope she will be with us later, but at the moment she is unwell and unable to join us for the first session at least and possibly also for the rest of the day. But we will confirm the position later. Meanwhile we consider it in the interests of justice to continue in her absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, before the witness comes in, 6D7112 [as interpreted] that was the black-and-white map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have now been informed that it has been replaced and that what is in the system now is the map that we showed on the ELMO in colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As long as you can satisfy Mr. Haider on these matters, then you will satisfy us. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Good morning, Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence will apply to it today until it's completed. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have very few questions left for you today. Yesterday during the course of your testimony you were shown an order which is Exhibit 6D700. You were asked to read a specific passage out which referred to tasks of the units of the 125th Brigade, motorised brigade, to support the MUP in an action along the axis of the villages of Likovac, Donje and Gornje Obrinje and Trdevac. You remember reading that out in court. And you recall that you said yesterday that you took part in this action which is envisaged in this order that I'm referring to, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I recognised Likovac, which is a locality that I remember in terms of having taken certain activities there. So my memory is linked to that locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. And the order that we're discussing was dated 24th September 1998, so I take it the actions that are -- the tasks that are envisaged in this order were carried out in the days following the issuing of the order, we're talking about 25th, 26th September 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in the order we saw that units of the 125th were being tasked to support your PJP company and also two other units of the MUP, the JSO and a PJP company from Kosovska Mitrovica. You recall these units being involved in this action along this axis?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, what I see here is the 125th BG/1. Their task was to support the attack of the 3rd OD PJP, which I assume is "odred," detachment. What I led was part of a company that was under me. Otherwise, what I said yesterday was that during these activities in Likovac I heard from my colleagues that six members of the company from Kosovska Mitrovica --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you there. I'm asking -- I was just asking about the units involved in the operation. You did explain that you heard that some members of the Kosovska Mitrovica company had been killed in this operation, yes, I recall that testimony.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So is it correct that the other MUP units involved in this operation would have been the PJPs from Kosovska Mitrovica and the JSO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the company from Kosovska Mitrovica, but I cannot confirm about the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any other MUP units with you in Likovac where you were deployed during the course of -- when this action was taking place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that there were other companies from my detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You don't recall exactly which other companies were involved in this action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really do not in view of the area of activity and also my dedication to my own tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did -- while you were carrying out this action were you primarily in Likovac or did you later move on to any of the other localities that are envisaged in this order? I'm talking about Donje and Gornje Obrinje and Trdevac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Focus of my activity was the road leading up to Likovac and the locality of Likovac itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know which MUP units that were involved in this action were deployed to the village of Gornje Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I really don't know about that locality either unless I see it here, in terms of units I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. And units of the VJ that were -- were there units of the VJ involved in this action that you were taking -- carrying out in the village of Likovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did notice some military personnel on the spot in Likovac, but I don't know whether they were involved in activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these would have been members of - I'm basing this on the order - members of the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed some military personnel. I cannot say anything about their identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of -- what were these military personnel doing? Were they providing support to the tasks that you were carrying out? What was their role?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When arriving from Likovac from the road, I did notice certain persons as individuals who were there in that village. So I did not notice them in terms of being involved in some activity but in terms of their presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. We have heard evidence in this case that during the course of an operation by Serb forces in this area, specifically in the village of Gornje Obrinje on 26th September 1998, 21 civilians, including a group of women and children, were killed. Do you have any information or have you heard about this killing taking place during the course of this operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, indeed not. I just heard about the death of those young men that I described a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that this massacre, alleged massacre, comes as news to you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you had received no prior information once this action was completed about what events happened in the village of Gornje Obrinje; that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we were not informed -- I was not informed, to be more precise, about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you -- your company engage in any combat in this action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until we arrived in Likovac, several times my unit was under fire from -- coming from the flanks. For the most part, from the nearby woods. If I'm -- if I remember correctly, it was 100 or 200 metres away from the road along which we were moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that really doesn't answer my question. Did you respond to that fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few times we did respond with fire when we noticed where it was that the source of firing at us was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you sustain any casualties, your company, your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My company did not sustain any losses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if you inflicted any injury on any of the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, since this was pretty far away, we just opened fire to protect ourselves, generally speaking; we fired into the air and we lay by the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you actually enter the village of Likovac on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my present-day recollections, I can confirm that we entered a built-up area that I heard was a locality called Likovac. I was told that it was called Likovac, and I know that there was a centre of this village and it was surrounded by some shops and a few houses. So if that can be considered as entering the village of Likovac, then that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you were told this by whom, that this was the village of Likovac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were there any civilians in the village when you entered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, it was empty, it was only members of the MUP who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know which date it was that you entered the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I really don't know. I know it was in September, I mean late in September, but I really don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you told us you recall this action taking place between 25th and 26th September, so it would be correct to say that the approximate date when you were in Likovac would be around those dates, 25th and 26th September?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can really only say to you that it was in the second half of September. It's been quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very short one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you once again. Mr. Paunovic, yesterday while my learned friend Ms. Kravetz was examining you, we heard a military term that appeared in conversation, although Ms. Kravetz I think put the question right. She asked you whether you were sent out for assistance. 6D682 is what I'd like to see on e-court, and you have the binder in front of you. This is a dispatch from the public security sector dated the 8th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you give me the number of the document once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6D682. Would you just read the first sentence, please, up until the first comma, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first paragraph: "The engagement of ..." "The engage of the members of the 37th and 87th Detachment of the PJP who on the 15th -- who were sent on the 15th of January, 1999, to assist the secretariat in Prizren," --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. His Honour Judge Bonomy asked you yesterday in relation to a term that was mentioned yesterday, and that was resubordination. Are MUP units resubordinated or are they sent out to render assistance; let's clear that first.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terminologically, the most correct way of putting it is that PJPs are sent out to help, to render assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at page 2 of this document. If you look at the signature, you worked at the police administration at that time. Whose signature is this underneath the name of Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I worked at the police administration from November 1998, not this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But this is February 1999.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I did work in the police administration. I think that this is Obrad Stevanovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to show you briefly 6D684. This is yet again a dispatch from the public security sector dated the 4th of February, 1999. Could you read out for us once again the first three lines from the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm reading it as follows: "The engagement of members of the 23rd and 73rd PJP Detachments from the SUP in Sremska Mitrovica, Pancevo, Zrenjanin, and Sombor, who were sent to help out the secretariat of the interior in Djakovica on the 11th of January, 1999, shall terminate on the 11th of February, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Further on it says: "Preparations for their replacement must be made and the following units should be sent to Djakovica on that day, according to establishment" --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I repeat this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I read it out. And then it says: "From the SUP in Novi Sad, 1st Company of the 23rd PJP Detachment ..." Do you know that at that time replacements were, indeed, taking place, that PJP units were being replaced in Kosovo, it's not that additional PJPs were being sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that was the case, that replacements were being sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 2 again, the signature, it says Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic. Whose signature this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of what I know, I think this is Obrad Stevanovic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we discussed the structure of PJPs in detail and we explained through different documents the legal structure, we heard about it all the way to the level of detachment commander. Who was the commander of PJPs and what was the name of the minister of interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior at that time was Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I knew, General Obrad Stevanovic was the commander of the PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you for having testified.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN PAUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Paunovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You're now free to leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Ljubivoje Joksic, and my colleague, Dan Ivetic, will be leading this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I should have recorded at the outset of this sitting the absence of Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Aleksic, I take it there is no objection at all to the proceedings continuing in his absence? I understand he's unwell and, in fact, at the moment being examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you're right. We shall have his consent during the day to press on in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, first of all, for the record, if you could please introduce yourself briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubivoje Joksic. I was born on 26th of January, 1949, in the village of Vranic, Barajevo municipality, Belgrade, Republic of Serbia. My father's name was Aleksandar and my mother's name was Milinka.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Did you have chance to give a statement, a written statement to the attorneys of the defence team of Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask the assistance of the usher to hand a hard copy of 6D1491 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, once you receive this document I would ask you to look at it and confirm whether in fact this is the statement that you gave to members of my team.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion in these past days to read and review this statement before signing it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I would ask you today to testify on these same topics, would your answers be the same as recorded herein?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for 6D1491 to be entered into evidence and would also ask for the following exhibits that are dealt with and detailed in the written statement to be put on the record as exhibits, those would be 6D139, 6D946, 6D142, 6D775, 6D776, 6D805, 6D990, 6D1002, 6D1003, 6D1004, 6D1005, 6D1006, 6D1007 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you maybe tell us which is the last one of the series?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last one of the series would be 6D1018 it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's 2 to 18?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct, and that brings me to the end of my list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to a portion of the statement, in particular paragraphs I think 2 through 42 sets forth in some detail information about the formation and creation of what eventually became the KLA, going back to 1960s and 1970s even. In some ways it's almost as though he's testifying as an expert on the KLA, but he's not been presented as an expert under Rule 94. The source of his information from the statement is rather vague. He does refer to RDB sources, secret documents which we don't have which we can't look at to compare and cross-examine him about, sources are the typical security services kinds of sources, I gather, insiders, informants, et cetera, which, as we all know, sometimes have issues of credibility. In many ways, Your Honour, I see this portion of his statement similar to portions of the statement of Mr. Tanic, who testified for the Prosecution, and to whom Mr. O'Sullivan and the Defence raised an objection and Your Honours decided to allow in only I think paragraphs 1 to 45 in his statement and directed the Prosecution to lead him live on other matters so that you could determine what weight to give his evidence that came from third-party sources or from hearsay. And so that's the basis of my objection to that portion of his statement. With regard to some of the exhibits contained therein, I have another objection. For example, in paragraph 54, Exhibit 6D805, the witness's statement said: "This is a JB document, public security document, it contains statistical data collected from the field. The information from this document is to my knowledge correct." That's rather vague to me, Your Honour. I could look at it and said, Well, to my knowledge it's incorrect. I think we need some further amplification before that exhibit gets admitted, and there are a few others like that. The ones that he helped prepare or the ones that he says were prepared by his boss who he worked closely with, I don't have any objection to. But the others that he says he has not seen before or he knows that a criminal report was filed in connection with it, that's not very enlightening and I don't know that standing alone is enough to allow for their admission at this point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can respond, I think I can work backwards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Some of the -- I think the criminal report that Mr. Hannis made reference to I believe is already an exhibit in this case and the witness was only commenting on the same in his statement. The extent of his knowledge and his testimony is contained in the statement, so we're not trying to expand upon that in any way. It is what it is and its evidentiary value is what the Trial Chamber will take it to be. With respect to 805, 6D805, it's a document giving information, data, relating to the time-period of the KLA activities and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I've lost you. What is the criminal report that you say Mr. Hannis referred to. I thought that was 6D805.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, 6D805 is an overview. I believe the criminal report that Mr. Hannis is making reference to would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I missed any reference to a criminal report in what Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just made reference to his speaking about a criminal report, that was in regard to paragraph 51, Exhibit 6D142. My particular objection regarding the objections -- regarding the exhibits, Your Honour, are in paragraphs 53, 54, and 55, Exhibits 6D776, 805, and 990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, I can verify that the criminal reports are items that are already in evidence that have been brought into evidence with Prosecution witnesses, for which we have had some testimony. We will have testimony from other Defence witnesses as well. The information from the RJB, the overviews of terrorist activities that Mr. Hannis mentions, the witness has confirmed his -- that the knowledge -- that the information contained therein is consistent with his knowledge from the RDB. That is of course open to the Office of the Prosecution to cross-examine upon to find out anything that they -- that they feel is important from that, just like any other witness. So I think it's -- that objection should be repelled insofar as he's just confirming the information and then it's open to the Prosecution to cross-examine him as to the factors behind that. So I don't see why that would require -- obviously, the man spent many years in Kosovo and Metohija working for the department of state security, so when he says that the information is correct with his knowledge, that implies it's from his official capacity as a person dealing exclusively with terrorism for a number of years, in fact, I think it was close to a decade. So if the Prosecution wish to cross-examine on that, by all means they're allowed to cross-examine on that. And I think there was one last issue which now I've lost in the transcript. I guess the general objection taken to the discussion of the KLA, again that's open to cross-examination by the Prosecution, and indeed if they feel that there is anything that is questionable or the source of it, I'm sure the witness can answer and then belay those fears, again as someone who spent ten years in Kosovo-Metohija -- approximately ten years I should say, working for the State Security Service, specifically dealing with terrorism, he's merely reciting facts, he's not opining as to any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You do remember taking objection to parts of the Tanic statement, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I personally did not do witness Tanic, so I wasn't even in court during most of that testimony, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will, therefore -- but you will have or remember taking objection to the statement of Abrahams?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But the -- the distinction I would make, sir, is that whereas this individual specifically was in -- was a -- was not a source for the RDB but actually was an officer in the RDB working on the terrain and is reporting on things that his service -- information that his service collected and events that, indeed, are talked about by other witnesses. A lot of this stuff has been confirmed by other witnesses and will be confirmed by other witnesses to come. So respectfully, we're not talking about someone who claims to be an operative of the RDB who is giving information that cannot be confirmed, this information can be confirmed and, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How can it be confirmed when it's information given by sources to him and these sources are varying kinds? Let me quote to you from your own objection to Abrahams. "The main problem is that a lot of his conclusions and findings are based upon the information he had at hand, and that is not necessarily the totality of the information available. Given that his information in his Rule 89(F) statement is culled from various reports, we do not know what portions are the result of things that he actually eye-witnessed or did research on or what was written by somebody else or what he heard from somebody or what he heard from an interviewee, for instance. So it's very difficult to discern what is first-hand history that he experienced and can report upon and what is second-hand history that he is reciting from some other source, of which we don't even know who that source is. We have no idea about the credibility or the credentials of the same." Now, what's the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the difference is, Your Honour, with Mr. Abrahams and his report we were talking principally about what purported witnesses told him and he was giving testimony that the -- the book was giving testimony about what other people said. We're giving testimony about events that occurred and that, in fact, the Office of the Prosecution should be well aware of these since one of their witnesses had the -- similar information relating to the same, one of the witnesses they did not call here today from the RDB, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not, I'm afraid, understanding the distinction at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There were -- yeah, if you go to paragraph 5 about political gatherings prior to 1982 and this idea of the Greater Albania and the key players in paragraph 6, and then paragraph 7 talking about the tribal system, it's all -- seems like expert evidence by somebody who may have researched it. And you'll remember that we've already had an expert, a military expert, Radinovic, part of whose report we excluded because it was based on sources that were really, from our point of view, unverifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the point with Radinovic, he was a military expert, not someone who had spent his entire employment dealing with terrorism. If there's a question about the sources, the gentleman is here to answer those questions. This is exclusively what he dealt with, the purview of his employment within the RDB was collection of this sort of information and would be the course of his employment -- the course of his activities on Kosovo -- in Kosovo-Metohija would be related directly to these matters. So if there's an issue of asking the witness questions about this, he's available to answer those, and he can verify the methods by which this information was collected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd prefer just to hear from the puppet rather than the puppet master as well. One person speaking at a time will be sufficient for our purposes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic, I don't think Mr. Ivetic has completed his submission. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I had completed my submission, just by saying he can verify the methods by which this information was collected, again from RDB -- from the RDB work method and the RDB presence on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One issue I contest is the allegation that I am able to examine the sources of his information. I can cross-examine him, but I don't have the sources of his information. In paragraph 2 in English in the middle he says: "The sources I have used for what I'm about to say in this statement are DB documents I have access to, intelligence and information collected from people who were infiltrated in terrorist groups, from colleagues, operative contacts, technology." We don't have those things, so we're going to have to live with what he says. He says, I looked at that, I read that document, I reviewed those intercepts, I talked to that infiltrator, and trust me when I tell you this is what it all means. We can't examine that. Your Honours, I would draw [Realtime transcript read in error "withdraw"] my analogy. You accepted the Defence arguments and kept out "As Seen, As Told." This statement paragraphs 2 through 45 or 42 could be called "As Read, As Heard"; it's no different. Matter of fact one difference is with regards to "As Seen, As Told" and "Under Orders," we actually brought into court some of those witnesses who had provided the information that went into those reports; we don't have that here, we have the author of this work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying "I withdraw my analogy" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I would draw an analogy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, yes sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- to "As Seen, As Told" and call this "As Read, As Heard." And if this is sufficient, then I would renew our motion to admit "As Seen, As Told" and "Under Orders." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make one further submission. If we want to do analogies, then I believe that the entire testimony of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic should be excluded on the same grounds since the military security service and the information provided by General Vasiljevic is, I would submit, identical to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to comment on that, Mr. Hannis, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I recall General Vasiljevic's testimony being fairly limited to the period of the war, April 1999, et cetera, he wasn't going back to the 1960s and 1970s, he was talking about meetings that he attended and he was talking about documents that he had and that he brought to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just a little more assistance you can give us, an example here, paragraph 25: "I have taken this information from a bulletin I had occasion to read ..." I mean, we would be a laughing stock as a Court to take that sort of specific statistical information from a witness based on a bulletin he had occasion to read which we don't have access to which we cannot challenged or explored or investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, 6D805 is, I believe, a bulletin on that topic, that's the exhibit that is also being produced -- the RJB overview of committed terrorist attacks on the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo-Metohija. I think that -- I think that's one of the -- I'm just looking at the list here since I don't have that exhibit in front of me, but -- and I submit, Your Honour, we've heard evidence from witnesses such as General Gajic, for instance, that the sole basis of his information was some unnamed source from Bosnia talking about what was going on in Kosovo. This man was on the ground the entire time and if there's a question about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, give me the page reference for Gajic because we're going to have to look at these things and decide what to do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I obviously can't give you the page reference for Gajic off the top of my head, but he testified with respect to the wolves from the Drina, that they were -- that the sole source for his information was from Bosnia, and that for the Skorpions, the sole source of his information was from Vojvodina, both of which are outside the territory of Kosovo-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's oral evidence that we are going to be able to deal with, much of it, no doubt, is going to be rejected. And one way of dealing with this may be to require the evidence, if you're insisting upon it, to be led orally, by identifying the parts of this statement that we would not be prepared to admit. That doesn't stop you trying to elicit the information from the witness by identifying his source and then leaving it to us to decide whether it should be admitted as authentic information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be great if I had the unlimited time that the Office of the Prosecution had to present their case, but I have a limited number of hours and therefore we were instructed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They didn't have unlimited time, Mr. Ivetic, and they had six cases to present, and you have been given a very generous allocation of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we were invited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, the other -- I was looking also at paragraph 24 at the same time. I ask myself what's the relevance of that. I mean, what is the relevance of that? I'm surprised that Mr. Hannis hasn't taken objection on the basis of relevance of a lot of this. Large chunks of it predate any period that we are really concerned about, and no doubt one can debate what has been happening in the region and in Kosovo in particular over a very long period of time and find it very interesting. But our decisions have to relate to 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your decisions have to relate to justice and having a totality of the picture on the ground that would impact upon making sure that justice is done in this courtroom. And in terms of the time-period, the time-period is chosen by the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So tell me the relevance of paragraph 24. I'm restraining myself from taking offence at the reference you've just made and the suggestion that we are not concerned with justice, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That was not the intention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I will lay that aside and ask you to tell me the relevance of paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The relevance is, Your Honour, that we've had evidence from Prosecution witnesses that the KLA did not exist during that time-period by showing the activities of the armed KLA during that time-period we confront --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's assume they did exist in 1993, what difference does it make to the decisions we've got to take?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should make an impact upon how you take the evidence presented by the Prosecution witnesses who said otherwise. It affects the credibility of the Prosecution witnesses who claimed there was no KLA -- there was no reason for the police or the army or anyone else to be in Kosovo-Metohija. It provides a totality of the environment that everyone had to live under in Kosovo-Metohija during the relevant time-period that is the part of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've lost me, I'm afraid, Mr. Ivetic. You think we've got to be concerned about the presence of the police in Kosovo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the time-period leading up to the period of the indictment demonstrates the atmosphere that was on the ground, the armed engagement with the KLA, the attacks by the KLA demonstrates what people were living under so you can understand their testimony that we've heard here during the periods of 1998 and 1999. And if you look at the -- well, if I could add to that, you look at some of the people that were involved in the attacks and when you take into account that they are in leading positions today in Kosovo-Metohija, it might also explain why witnesses coming from that region today only give favourable evidence about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I for one am surprised that you think that it is a valuable use of your resources to present all this pre-1996 material. It is a complicated issue, this, and we will have to, I think, adjourn to make a decision about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you go, Your Honour, I have one specific further objection to paragraph 54, Exhibit 6D805. It doesn't appear to be in e-court. I haven't seen the document yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova has had the same problem, we can't find this document, which you think may even be the bulletin referred to in paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Without having it in front of me, that's what I'm reading off of a list that's in front of me that my colleague is checking right now. It should be in there. It's -- it's released. I believe that's the only document we don't have a translation for, that might be the -- that might be the issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Joksic, we are going to have to adjourn to decide how much of this statement we will admit, and then we will proceed with your evidence. We will return as quickly as we can. At the moment I cannot tell you how long it will take us to make that decision. --- Break taken at 10.08 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The record should reflect that Judge Nosworthy is now with us. Conscious of your time constraint point, Mr. Ivetic, we've done this as quickly as we possibly could. We hope that we've done justice to the issue, although dealing with it quickly. We propose to exclude from this statement a number of paragraphs, but some are being excluded because we consider oral evidence should be given on the topic so that we have an understanding of the source of the information because it does seem of direct relevance to us. However, paragraphs 3, 4, 5 will be excluded. These have the appearance of expert evidence in relation to a period that we are not concerned with and the witness has not been qualified to us as an expert. On the same basis we shall exclude paragraphs 8, 9, and 10. We consider that paragraphs 15 and 16 relate to matters of some relevance, but we do not propose to allow that evidence to be presented through this statement, so we will exclude 15 and 16 for that reason. Similarly, paragraph 22 will be excluded. We consider -- 22, 24, and 25 for the same reason. We will exclude 23 because it is, in our opinion, irrelevant, as are paragraphs 26, 27, and 28, and we shall exclude paragraph 41 on the basis that if that evidence is to be presented it should be presented viva voce, that's similar to the other exclusions we have made. That's all the limited damage we have done to your statement, Mr. Ivetic. As a result, you should file a revised version of the statement and you should do that by Monday, close of business, so that we have this before the Court by the time the witness is likely to be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "revised," should it be redacted so that the paragraph numbers stay the same?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The paragraph -- yes, the paragraph numbers can remain as they are, but -- well -- yes, they have to remain as they are, otherwise the record will be difficult to align, unless you were able to do it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will do that within the time-period you have given us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I should also record that while we had adjourned I asked one of the staff to speak to you to check the period in which the witness was engaged in Kosovo and you indicated that was from sometime in 1991 until 1999. We had wrongly assumed it was in the statement, but when we retired we found that it was not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just so there's no doubt, that's the area I was going to ask the witness to give us information on so we can have the precise dates, et cetera for the completeness of information before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may yet have at least one other witness in relation to whose evidence we suspect a similar problem may arise. We hope this has been a learning experience, because as you have pointed out, the last thing you want to be doing is using your time to deal with issues of this nature. So you should be conscious of that and we are open to ingenious methods of resolving these issues out of court if you can get together with the Prosecution where you envisage such a problem arising. That means we can continue with the evidence, but it's probably a bit unrealistic to start again just at this minute since we are going to again almost immediately have a break. So we'll resume at ten past 11.00 if everyone can arrange to do that. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, we have an official break at this time. Our timing's particularly unfortunate this morning, so again I have to ask you to leave the courtroom and we'll see you again at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Joksic, we should be up and running now. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, could you first just briefly tell us a summary of your employment within the service later renamed the department of state security, including your assignment to Kosovo-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I worked with the state security from the 1st of June, 1977, until the 1st of November, 2001, which was when I retired after 40 years of employment. Between 1977 and 1984, I was an operative officer with the state security. Between 1984 and 1989 I was the head of a group in the State Security Service. In 1989 I became the deputy head of an administration. In 1991, December 1991, the 18th of December, I was dispatched by the central office of the service to Kosovo-Metohija, where I was appointed head of the third sector of the local service of the state security. I worked as the head of sector of this local office until the 1st of May, 2002, which is when the service itself was revamped and three security centres were established in Kosovo and Metohija. On 1st of May I was appointed assistant coordinator of the State Security Service for Kosovo and Metohija. It was called the state security sector by this time. I was appointed assistant and I was in charge of anti-terrorism and extremism in Kosovo and Metohija and jobs and tasks related to those problems. I remained in that position until the 1st of July, 1999. The 1st of July, 1999, from that time to the time I retired, I was the special advisor to the chief of the sector, state security sector, and I was in charge of problems related to Albanian terrorism and the extremism in Kosovo and Metohija and in Serbia south as well. I didn't state that explicitly in my statement, but I would like to point that out because I realized that some of the paragraphs are being stricken from my statement. Just for the sake of clarity, I was in Kosovo and Metohija also in 1983. I was down there because of the serious situation in terms of security in Kosovo and Metohija. There were very destructive rallies in 1981 and we had been dispatched from the then-Yugoslavia, the operatives that we were, we were dispatched there to assist because those were republican services and we went through the Federal Ministry of the Interior, or rather, the State Security Service and we were dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija to assist them over there. I was in what used to be the Pristina section of the State Security Service as an operative officer, and I assisted with dealing with various problems that were quite serious at the time, emerging problems in Kosovo and Metohija. This was still the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and these operatives were from all the republics, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Macedonia and Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, if Mr. Ivetic wants to explore that, he will ask questions about that, if there are objections to these we'll deal with them, but at the moment 1983 does not seem relevant to this Court, so let's proceed to things that are. And one date can't be right in that account you've given, the 1st of May, 2002, has appeared as the date that you became involved or in charge of anti-terrorism and extremism, and that can't be correct. What was the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the 1st of May I was in charge of those tasks, but I was the chief of the third sector of the local service of state security, and then as of the 1st of May I became assistant coordinator for the whole of Kosovo and Metohija. I was coordinating the work of all three state security centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is in the year --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2002, as the witness says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how does that tie in with leaving Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rather, or rather, I apologise, 1992, 1992. I don't think I was that far wrong, about ten years perhaps. 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But when did he retire? I think he says after 40 years and over there he says November 2001, so I couldn't reconcile that in perhaps 20 -- paragraph -- page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He can answer that, I guess, if there's confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Mr. Joksic, when did you retire exactly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: 2001, the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Why does he say 40 years, after 40 years of service? I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we have special terms in our service. We have four months every year, that counts extra, so 30 years would equal to a total of 40 years. So I had earned by this time 40 years and two months of employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If that satisfies Your Honours, I can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, can you tell us how the work and functioning of the state security department was regulated, what laws regulated that work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The State Security Service, where I was working, works under the constitution and under the Law on the Interior as well as our own Rules of Service. Those would be the rules and laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who headed the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: At the head of the RDB there was the head of service, he had his deputies and assistants, sometimes more assistants, sometimes fewer, but at least two or three at any given time. Under that in the RDB we had administrations with heads of administrations and their deputies and assistants, and this was in the central office of the service. And then as of 1992 there were state security sector centres, in Serbia and Kosovo-Metohija there were a total of 19 of those. At the head of those centres there were the centre heads, deputy centre heads, assistant centre heads. And further down we had sector chiefs, heads of groups, local offices and detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us, sir. And with respect to the management of the RDB, if I can turn to P1192, which would be the rules of the internal organization of the RDB, Article 44, which will be at page 14 to 15 in the B/C/S and page 14 in the English. And I would ask you, sir, once the page comes up with -- at the bottom -- it will be on the bottom of the page, I guess the 15th page in B/C/S, and going on to the 16th page. To save time, sir, if you could review Article 14 [sic] and tell me, Does that accurately reflect in detail the management or "rukovodjenje" of the RDB? Article 44. I believe the transcript says 14, that was the reference to the page number in English.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I do have my glasses on but this is still very difficult for me to read. Despite my glasses, it's very difficult for me to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a hard copy but it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps now I could now that we have managed to zoom in. Yes, this has been zoomed in on and I can tell you now -- yeah, it's precisely what I was saying. That's what the article of the Rules of Service reflects.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us a little bit about the method by which information was circulated upwards within the RDB, and if need be, we can reference to the rule book if you have any specific references for us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The State Security Service, as I said, worked based on the constitution, the laws, and the Rules of Service in order to protect the constitutional order of the country. We would uncover any crimes and criminal offences that put the constitutional order of the country at risk. The principal information worked like this, the lowest-level units the state security centres up to the headquarters, the central office, the headquarters, where this information was sorted and instructions were issued as to how to proceed on these specific jobs that we were doing. The peculiar nature of passing information along in Kosovo and Metohija was this, there was the coordinator and we were his assistants; therefore, there was a single copy of each report in addition to being sent to the central office and the administrations, one copy was always received by us, the team of coordinators, and the reason we did this, the same type of problems prevailed throughout Kosovo and Metohija at the time. And this was in order to coordinate all three centres because the same types of problems recurred in Prizren, Pristina, and Gnjilane in order to avoid mistakes and in order to not do anything or take any measures that weren't coordinated throughout the service in Kosovo and Metohija. It was for that reason that the position of a coordinator was established as well as that of his assistants. So one copy of this report was always dispatched to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now if you could tell us, please, with respect to the issuance of criminal denunciations against suspects, what was the role and duty of the RDB especially vis-a-vis other organs such as investigative judges or prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Once a crime was uncovered by the service, especially crimes to do with terrorism and extremism, the state service would look into those incidents and once perpetrators were found the State Security Service would do the preliminary investigation, they would interview those people, they would take their statements, they would file these away and cross-reference all this information. Based on this, a criminal complaint would be filed, which was then submitted to the prosecutor and the investigating judge. Our cooperation with the office of the prosecutor, the investigating judges, and all the other security players proceeded along the lines established by the instructions on our working cooperation with all these other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript. Once the criminal denunciation is issued by the department of state security, who -- who or what dictates the further role of your service regarding any further criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: As for any further criminal investigation, there has to be a request by the prosecutor or the investigating judge and only then could we collect or gather information in order to amend or supplement any situations that weren't entirely clear in the criminal report itself, but only pursuant to a request by the investigating judge or the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us a little bit of the details of the structure of the state security department in Kosovo-Metohija during -- from 1992 onwards, since you mention that the service was revamped in 1992.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: After the service was restructured in Kosovo-Metohija, there were three centres of the state security sector, the Pristina one, the Gnjilane one, and the Prizren one. Each centre comprised sections, therefore, in the Pristina centre there was the Kosovska Mitrovica section; in Prizren, Djakovica and Pec; and in Gnjilane, Urosevac. Instead of the seven that there were earlier, now we had three centres of state security sector. Within these centres, in addition to these sections, there were other offices. First we called them detachments and then later we called them local branches. For example, in Pristina there were Lipljan, Obilic, Podujevo and there was a forward operations team in Kosovo Polje. In Kosovska Mitrovica there were the local branches within the section in Kosovska Mitrovica, in Vucitrn and Srbica. And then in Pec, in Istok and Klina. In Prizren, Suva Reka. In Gnjilane, Vitina, Kosovska Kamenica, Stimlje. So those were the lowest-ranking ones, detachments, as the rule said, and later they were called local offices or local branches of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these various organs that you have identified of the RDB, were these centres, departments, detachments, and operative groups subordinate to the SUPs or OUPs or police stations or were they autonomous from the RJB -- from the RJB organs on the same territory?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: As is well-known, the state security sector was within the Ministry of the Interior, but those were separate, special organizational units. Therefore, in its entirety the management in the State Security Service and the reporting only proceeded within the state security sector itself. No one from the state security sector was ever in charge of anything in the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask him to repeat the last part of his answer. The transcript says that no one from state security was ever in charge of anything in state security. If I could just have him repeat what he actually said rather than ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No one in charge from -- no one from the public security sector was in charge of anything or could issue any orders in the state security sector. It all went from the chief and then down to the lowest-ranking people within the state security sector and not outside it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that cleared it up without me prompting any correction. Now, with respect to the various organs, was there -- you mentioned Suva Reka. What was in Suva Reka and how large was that organ of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In Suva Reka there was a detachment, what was later called a local office or a local branch. There were two or three operative offices there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence that the witness said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have already talked about how information was sent up by the various organs of the RDB and that a copy was sent always to Pristina. Can you tell us why a copy in parallel was always sent to the CRDB in Pristina, what were the reasons for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: This copy was not submitted to Pristina all the time, but we were in the same building as the CRDB of Pristina, so it was sent to us, the coordinators, and the reason was, I said that a while ago when I explained the function of the service, because the leaders of the state security sector decided that they should establish some coordinators and their assistants in Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, a coordinator and his assistants in Kosovo and Metohija, because the type of problems faced by the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was the same. So we also had -- well, I'm just naming one example of terrorism in Pec, Pristina, and Kosovska Mitrovica, so that a copy was received of all these documents that were assembled and we as coordinators would familiarize ourselves with the situation throughout Kosovo and Metohija, and from there we would work together with the line services and the central offices and we would coordinate with them and we would issue instructions on what to do and how to proceed and how certain actions should be coordinated and combined in order to track down perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've perhaps misunderstood something there, line 23: "This copy was not submitted to Pristina all the time, but we were in the same building as the CRDB of Pristina..." What is the CRDB? Is it not the coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I believe the -- well, we can ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is the CRDB of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The CRDB of Pristina is the central security sector in Pristina that worked there and it covered the territory of Pristina municipality and Mitrovica municipality, and we were in the same building but we were the coordinators. We didn't belong to the CRDB of Pristina, we were the coordinators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the service, the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if you could tell us who were the coordinators in, let's begin with 1998, that were in Pristina from the RDB.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 until the end of 1998 the chief coordinator was David Gajic. I was his assistant. And between 1992 and 1999 we had another assistant who was dealing with counter-intelligence, but this person was not always the same. Several different people came and went. David Gajic and I were always there since 1992. He stayed until the end of 1998 and I stayed until the end of -- until my departure from Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And before we go on to -- well, let me ask you this question: Can you tell us the ethnic or national structure of the membership of the employees of the RDB in Kosovo-Metohija during 1998/1999, what ethnic groups were represented and working in the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, there were all the different ethnicities living in Kosovo in the RDB, Serbs, Albanians, Muslims, and others who were there were involved, the Roma and so on and so forth. Although in those years, for example, if you take the Pristina centre, the RDB Pristina centre, there were about 30 per cent Albanians, 70 per cent Serbs and other. The other two centres, there was a smaller percentage but there were Albanians involved and other ethnicities too. I can't give you the exact breakdown in terms of percentage, but I know in Pristina it was 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned that David Gajic stayed on as the chief coordinator until 1999. Can you tell us who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: He was chief coordinator until the end of 1998. From the 1st of January, 1999 on, it was Miso Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the head coordinator in Pristina, whether it was David Gajic or Mr. Vilotic, to whom would they report? Who was their immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Their immediate superior was the head of RDB, until 1998 Mico [as interpreted] Stanisic, and from the end of 1998 Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And who managed the RDB's work at the level of the centres of security out in the field?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The leaders of the centre were heads of the RDB, and they had deputies and assistants. If you want me to say specifically how it was in relation to Kosovo and Metohija, the chief of the Pristina RDB centre was Milan Lakovic; the chief of the one in Prizren, Milivoj Savic; and the one the chief of the one in Gnjilane, Bozidar Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you, you've already mentioned the level of -- excuse me, you've mentioned the issue of the RJB and the RDB as being separate services. Could you focus for the moment on an organ called the MUP staff in Pristina. Were any RDB structures or organs from Kosovo-Metohija subordinated in any way or answering to the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No one from the RDB was subordinated or in any way answered to the MUP staff in Pristina. As for these MUP staffs and the SUPs, we only had cooperation. We worked together pursuant to instructions relayed to us by the minister, cooperation on exchanging intelligence in our struggle against terrorism. There was no system of SUP subordination, no hierarchy; it was cooperation and it was exchange of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, Your Honour, my colleagues point to a error in the transcript in page 39, line 11, Mico Stanisic should be Jovan -- Jovica Stanisic, there are two individuals with the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can -- you've discussed that. If I can ask specifically, were either Mr. David Gajic or Mr. Milos Vilotic members of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, it's not Milos, it's Milisav Vilotic. According to my information, they were never members of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about an employee of the RDB known as Milorad Ulemek Lukovic, also sometimes also known as Legija, was he a member of the MUP staff in Pristina and if you could specifically tell us upon what you base your information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware whether he was a member or not. I don't think he was and the reason I think that is that I was always there and I never saw him attending any meetings or coming to the staff. I saw him maybe two or three times in the course of 1998/1999 when the minister of the interior or another high-ranking politician came to Kosovo and then I saw Milorad Lukovic, Legija, two or three times, on two or three occasions, but never at staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us whether it was the practice of the RDB to keep a written record of assignments of its employees in the field, that is to say the posts that they were assigned to in the field?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, every operative or employee of the security service received a document giving him his schedule, his deployment on the terrain, and this would be kept in his personnel file, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, to save time, we would be submitting Exhibits 6D302 and 6D303 at this time, for which I believe there are official translations. These would be the personal dossiers of Messrs. Gajic and Vilotic, which speak for themselves as to the posts and assignments held by these persons. I will not belabour the point and make any arguments or submissions at this time, but when the time is right I will rely on these documents to frame arguments or conclusions therefrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, that sounds like a suggestion that these will be tendered in a motion in due course. Are you familiar with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are they documents we should admit just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any objection to -- I mean, they appear authentic on their face. I have some submissions to make on them, maybe some questions to ask about them. I don't object to them being admitted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will admit these two documents and save you the labour, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And a specific question for you, under the existing rules, laws, and method of work of the RDB, could Sreten Lukic, then a general, as manager, or "rukovodilac," or head of the MUP staff and as a member of the RJB command or issue orders to the members of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now just a slightly different question as a factual matter. Did Sreten Lukic ever command over or issue orders to RDB members in Kosovo-Metohija in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now to clear up just a few more things. I'd like to turn to the JSO, the special operation unit. Did Sreten Lukic participate in the forming of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Sreten Lukic could not have participated in the forming of the JSO and he didn't. That unit - and I know this because I was a member of the service - was established in 1996 or 1997. At that time Sreten Lukic was assistant of the city secretary for the interior of the city of Belgrade and he had nothing to do either with the unit or with the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, has Sreten Lukic ever been a member of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, never, to the best of my knowledge, and I think I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that the JSO was exclusively within the domain of the RDB, as set forth by Article 5 of the rule of the RDB, which is the exhibit that we had, P1192?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The unit for special operations was a separate unit within a State Security Service, it was a separate organ which was under the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you about another individual. Was Goran Radosavljevic, also known as Guri, ever in command of the JSO or any part thereof?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Goran Radosavljevic, Guri, was a member of the public security sector; and to the best of my knowledge, he never commanded either part of a JSO unit or an entire JSO unit. As far as I know, he was only a member of the staff in charge of training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the JSO ever based in Kosovo Polje during 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the course of 1998 and 1999, the JSO was stationed in Kosovo Polje in a privately owned company, I can't remember what it was called now, that's where it was located. And as far as I know their commander was Zivko Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think there's translation issue. You've mentioned Zivko Trajkovic in Kosovo Polje. Are you talking about the SAJ or the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The SAJ, that's what I'm talking about, it was the SAJ. The JSO was never in Kosovo Polje. It was the SAJ, and their commander was Zivko Trajkovic. I thought you were asking me about the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you also think that in relation to the question about Radosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question for me? Yes, yes, Radosavljevic had nothing to do with either the SAJ or the JSO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know now, Mr. Ivetic, whether the witness was referring to the right organization throughout that exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can ask him again to make it simplified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me focus first of all with the JSO, which you said was an organ -- a separate unit under the RDB. Was Goran Radosavljevic, Guri, ever connected in any way with the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we could turn to the RJB side of things. To your knowledge, was Goran Radosavljevic, Guri, ever connected in any way to the special anti-terrorist unit, or SAJ?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified a station in Kosovo Polje. Which specific unit was stationed in Kosovo Polje and which structure of the MUP did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The SAJ was a special unit of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, sir, could you tell us during 1998 and 1999 where in Kosovo was the JSO of the RDB based?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: We as members of the RDB and coordinators in Kosovo and Metohija had no connection with that unit; however, to the best of my knowledge, it was stationed some 4 or 5 kilometres away from Kosovska Mitrovica. The unit was directly linked to the chief of the service, and they had almost no connection with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us a little bit more about the precise command structure as you know it of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, that unit had its commander and deputy commander. I'm not aware of the lower-down chain of command, and it was responsible directly to the chief of the RDB, who was the only one who could use that unit or issue an order to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could anyone from the RDB in Kosovo, that is to say any of the coordinators or heads of the centres, affect the assignments or engagements of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, no one could. In a previous period, before 1998 and 1999, before the major fighting and operations, we as members of the service could ask the chief of the RDB if we were carrying out a complex action to have a part of the JSO engaged in it. That's what I can remember, and I think this occurred on only two or three occasions throughout my stay in Kosovo-Metohija from 1992 to 1999. It may have happened a few times in 1996 and 1997 when we asked for that unit to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mention in paragraph 50 of your written statement a criminal denunciation against a member of the reserve JSO in Kosovska Mitrovica, Mr. Veselinovic, Goran. Do you have knowledge of any criminal acts perpetrated by members of the JSO in Kosovo in 1999 apart from this -- the criminal act set forth in paragraph 50 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any other crimes committed by members of the JSO in Kosovo in the course of 1999, and as for this criminal report it was shown to me and I saw it and I heard about the events at the time and I was also shown the report when I was being proofed. To the best of my knowledge, this person was a reserve officer, not an active-duty member of the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can now move on to another topic. Based upon your information in the field, did the public security service utilise paramilitary formations or parapolice formations in Kosovo and Metohija during 1999 -- or I should say at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, as far as I know, from the SDB, the RDB did not use such paramilitary units, nor were such units present in Kosovo-Metohija to the best of my knowledge. I even learned from the chief of the RDB, who contacted us, we were told that should such forces turn up we should not accept any of them. If there were any volunteers, they should report to the Yugoslav Army, who would then see whether they could join their units or not. But no other formations could be included in the police, apart from the regular and reserve police forces of the RJB. I had this order personally, I received it from the chief of the RDB, and these were instructions in case such units turned up, but to the best of my knowledge there were no such units there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, we've had a bit of evidence from people living in Kosovo at the time about activities by people described as paramilitaries who, on the basis of these descriptions, were acting in a way that it was inappropriate for someone in the military to be acting. And on some of these occasions it's actually sounded as though these were scruffy individuals that you would not expect to see in an army. Now, of course if there was no one like that acting violently in Kosovo and forces are proved -- forces of some description wearing uniforms are proved to have committed an atrocity, then the finger would be pointing at official forces of the state, if that was established.
