So it's a big issue for us to know if there were paramilitary personnel or parapolice personnel operating in 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo. It's not uncommon in this court for witnesses to hide behind regulations and rules and tell us -- give us an answer based on what ought to happen because the rules say so. And you're a man obviously whose life to some extent during this period was regulated, but you're also a man who is being presented to us as one with his ear to the ground, who knows the score in Kosovo. Against all that background, are you telling us that to the best of your knowledge there were no paramilitary personnel acting in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind the wartime situation in Kosovo and Metohija and the overall security situation, apart from unofficial information which I received about a group turning up in Podujevo and committing some crimes there, and I was told that they had been immediately expelled from Kosovo and Metohija, I did not learn of any other groups turning up in Kosovo and Metohija from official sources. And as for this one group I heard about, I heard about it unofficially. The information was that a group had turned up in Podujevo and that they had immediately been expelled from Kosovo and Metohija. In the post-war period, in 2001, I read in the press who these people had been. But at the time I didn't know what group it was that had turned up in that part of Kosovo and Metohija, in Podujevo, that is, right after you crossed the administrative border with Serbia. That's all I heard about, and I didn't find out until after the war who these people had been. Then I read in the papers that proceedings had been instituted against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the RDB have any information about the participation of any group called the Wolves from the Drina having a base in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I think I mentioned this in a previous response. I know that in Kosovo Polje there was an SAJ unit which was stationed there. As we in Kosovo Polje, and I personally, both in 1998 and 1999, often went there because there were many restaurants there where we could go and have a bite to eat, and then we would pass by that privately owned company where the SAJ was stationed. I never observed any other men there who -- apart from members of the SAJ. I remember that building, it was a privately owned company trading in beer and other things, but I can't remember the name of the company now. We often went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, that was a very simple question about one organization, alleged organization, called the Wolves from the Drina, and the simple question was: Did you have any information about their participation in Kosovo Polje. Now, is the answer to that no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As within his position as the head of the department of state security, could Rade Markovic send personnel or assign personnel to positions in Kosovo and Metohija within RJB organs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, he couldn't. He could only send personnel to the JSO, which was part of the RDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to -- for the moment to the time-period of the NATO bombings. Could you tell us about the impact or effect that the NATO bombings had on the work of the RJB and RDB in Pristina as you witnessed it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: After the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, all conditions for the normal work of the SDB [as interpreted] and the SJB were lost. As the SJB building was destroyed, the entire service as well as the RDB moved out of their official premises in Pristina, so that the centre was now distributed in several concealed locations, hidden locations, around town, in cellars, in companies, and also the RJB had to do the same, both because of operative information we had that certain premises would be bombed, we had to hide and look for other locations, but also because of the KLA activities. We had information that they would be entering town, perpetrating assassinations and so on, and that employees of the RJB would be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to communications between yourselves and the organs in the field, how were those impacted or affected after the commencement of the NATO air war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of NATO air-strikes, after the first bombs fell, communications were for the most part interrupted. I can tell you, for example, that with the centre in Pec and Prizren we had almost no communication throughout the war. We could have communications when the chief of the centre in Pristina [as interpreted] managed to reach us in Pristina personally, bringing us information and telling us what was going on in that area. The main aims inter alia of the NATO air-strikes, the main targets, were the telecommunications systems in Kosovo and Metohija, and these were bombed daily. In Pristina there was a constant air-raid alert which never stopped for the entire period of 78 days, and we all lived in specific conditions. As for your specific question concerning communications, it would depend on couriers getting through or the chief coming to see us personally, bringing us the latest information, either in writing or orally, and then we could pass that on to the service headquarters for their use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood you earlier. I thought the three centres in Kosovo were Pristina, Prizren, and Gnjilane. Was Pec also a centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That was a department of the Prizren centre, so it came under the Prizren centre; but that was the department with which we had almost no communication throughout the war, I mean by telephone. We had to use couriers or other means to communicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed, at page 50, line 6, I believe he said the chief of the centre in Prizren, that can be easily verified on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct from my recollection, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Pristina, do you recall any civilian targets hit or affected negatively by the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Pristina I was there. First the post office was bombed and then a street right next to the post office inhabited by civilians mostly of Turkish ethnicity was bombed, then the Jugopetrol warehouse and the Beopetrol warehouse, Devet Jugovica, at the exit from Pristina and then some transformer stations bringing electric power to Pristina were also bombed. All of this created a very difficult situation because there was no electricity, there was no water, there were no staple foodstuffs, and the population was in a hopeless situation, the entire population. And no newspapers arrived, so we couldn't get information as to what was going on. All we could do was try to tune into a satellite television station, and then we would hear what was going on throughout Serbia from foreign stations, foreign broadcasters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the information that was available to you, during the entire course of the war until you withdrew from Kosovo, did you at any time receive any information relating to any massacre of civilians in Suva Reka or any indications of involvement of an RDB employee, Mr. Niksevic [sic] in the same?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: During the war we had not received any information about what had happened in Suva Reka. What is particularly surprising as far as I'm concerned - and I learned many things only after the war later in Belgrade. But I find it strange that we were not aware of that information because the Prizren chief of security was rather vigilant and we received most of our information from him during the course of the war from the centre in Prizren. However, as for what happened in Suva Reka, I didn't know about that until we got out of Kosovo, and it was only in the later period that I found out from the press and the other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned the NATO -- the effect of the NATO bombings on the utilities. What was the atmosphere like in Pristina during the time-period of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the atmosphere, it was quite difficult there. Serbs, Albanians, and all other people living there were quite frightened. Many people started leaving Pristina, people of all ethnic backgrounds. Albanians started leaving in the direction of Albania and Kosovo, or rather, Macedonia and Skoplje, and the other population, non-Albanian, towards Serbia. Most of the Serbs had already transferred their women and children to Serbia once the bombing started, and after the bombing started Albanians started going en masse towards Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard of the existence of any so-called Operation Horseshoe planned by the Yugoslav and Serbian authorities to expel all Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija, as some of the Prosecution's evidence has alleged?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: First of all, I claim with certainty that the state security sector did not know of any such action or operation being planned. We had received intelligence to the effect that some foreign agencies, specifically the German intelligence agency, had released that false information in order for it to have a psychological effect on the Albanian population. Later on, after the war, I read somewhere that a German general confessed himself that this was in fact a false information that they had provided, that there was this Operation Horseshoe. I don't know and the State Security Service does not know of the existence of any such operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Witness Veton Surroi claimed that the late David Gajic of the RDB threatened of the existence of a plan called Scorched Earth, or "Sprzena Zemlja" in Serbian, to eliminate Albanians from Kosovo. Did any such plan under that name or any other name with that goal in mind exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a page reference to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a serious objection, counsel? It's in the statement I believe of the -- well, let me find it. It's going to take some time. If I could skip that question and move on and I can get the page number, because I'm positive I remember that being expressly utilised, but for the sake of efficiency I'll move on. I don't know when we have the next break coming up, but I suspect that I will be able to have just a few more questions after that break and I can bring that up at that point in time with the references to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very helpful, Mr. Ivetic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the relationship and cooperation between the RDB and the Army of Yugoslavia's security service, formally known as KOS and now I believe known as the VB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, cooperation between the state security and the security service of the army was in my assessment always a good one. We cooperated and exchanged information. Often officers of the military service came to us for an exchange of information, and in my assessment and in the assessment of the then-officials of the service, this cooperation was a correct and good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During 1999 were you aware of any, I'll say differences of opinion or bickering between the heads of the RDB and military security service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I was not aware of that. My assessment was from down there that we had correct, proper cooperation with the military intelligence. I didn't know about that. While preparing for this testimony I saw some documents that spoke otherwise, but I think that what these documents say is not correct. At that time, in 1999, I was not aware of these documents. It was only now when I was preparing for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask for other microphones to be switched off while the witness is speaking. We have great difficulty hearing him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see we're getting a note from the interpreters. I will endeavour to keep my microphone off when he's answering. I did switch to this other microphone since the other one was making more static from the computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I would like to ask you about another topic, the KVM, the Kosovo Verification Mission, of the OSCE. Did the RDB have any information about members of this mission having any ulterior missions with other -- with the security services or intelligence services of other countries; and if so, what was that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the State Security Service, when the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived down there, placed a number of the members of this mission under control because we assumed since these were former military officers of the western countries that were -- that they were members of the intelligence agencies of the countries that they were coming for. So the service, the RDB, took all measures in order to see what else they were doing in addition to the tasks that the Kosovo Verification Mission had. We learned quite a few interesting things in the process. In some situations they were instructors to members of the KLA. They gave them advice as to how they should act, where they should hide, when to attack, when not to attack, and so on and so forth. There were things like that and quite a bit of information was written about that. This was specific information that we got by placing our own collaborators among them through intelligence technical measures, that is to say through listening in on their conversations and applying other methods that the service used. We thereby learned that they were actually acting as advisors, or rather, instructors to the terrorist organization of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the RDB have any such information relating to Shaun Byrnes, head of the US-KDOM?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, we do have that information in relation to Shaun Byrnes. We had specifically some of his contacts with KLA commanders and brigades. We also have information out there that is an integral part of a statement in the investigative proceedings where he was giving them advice. I remember this particular unit in the Lab area, and he was saying that they were well-equipped, well-trained, and that they should keep it for the future and they should withdraw it now so that this unit would not engage the military and the police, they should keep it for the future. We from the service knew what this future meant because we were aware of the plans of the KLA to carry out the infamous Kosovo spring because they knew that a major offensive was being prepared in the spring of 1998 -- 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The infamous Kosovo spring offensive being prepared, who was it being prepared by and against whom, according to the information of the RDB?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: According to our information this offensive was being prepared against the Serb forces, or rather, the army and police in Kosovo and Metohija, and what they were planning in particular was -- well, actually by then they had already had promises from NATO members, or rather, from the foreign factor of the west that they should secure unhindered entry for NATO forces via Albania. One of their main plans was that they should make it possible for them to attack the Serb forces on the border with Albania, in the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can look at some specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for 6D201 to be called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, while we're getting the page zoomed in on at this moment, could you tell us what kind of document is this and was it the type that would be prepared by your service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, it should be enlarged a bit more. I see that it's a document, it's an operative information from the Pristina centre of the state security. It just needs to be enlarged if I need to interpret this further. Yes, yes, that is information from the centre of state security of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, sir, if you have knowledge of how such information would be collected and who -- what this means on the title when it talks about Bardhyl Mahmuti?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, information of this kind was collected by applying all methods that the service uses in its work. As I've already said, these are interviews, infiltration of our collaborators to deal with those that were being monitored by the service, also by applying technical measures. At the time when quite a few of these terrorist actions were being carried out, we received information by arresting some of the participants in these informations, and while investigating them, interrogating them, we got quite a bit of information about the KLA. So roughly these would be all the sources of our information regarding this and that is the information that the State Security Service provided further on. This included interrogations of arrested persons who were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, was any complaint made to the KVM about positive assistance being given to KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any such thing. We as the State Security Service, we informed the leadership and the members of the military and the public security; and now whether they were further told anything else, that I cannot tell you, given the level that I was at down there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would be interested to see any documents relating to complaints of assistance. I think this is a very wide-ranging complaint, but it does seem to lack any particular substance that we could make findings on. The activities of someone who was in KDOM is one thing, but the activities of the KVM are another. Is there anything specific on this, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In terms of activities of persons, that would be important to our case. Shaun Byrnes is a witness in these proceedings for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But we also have clear evidence of the refusal, we've got to decide whether to suspect it or not, but the refusal of KDOM to integrate with the KVM. The question I'm asking is related to positive assistance being given by personnel who were introduced as part of the KVM to Albanians who had ill-will towards the Serb forces. And if there was such evidence, it would be I think on the face of it surprising if it was not raised in the constant liaison meetings that were taking place between the KVM and the various bodies involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Having in mind my witness list, I think you will be rest assured that there will be evidence led on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About actual complaints being made as part of the liaising?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One of the witnesses we have coming hopefully this week or the beginning of next week was in fact Mr. Mijatovic who had all the daily meetings with the KVM and so you will be able to ask him precisely about that aspect of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, one question which I wish to ask is: How many times such complaints were made? Have you any knowledge of it? Was it a recurring thing or at some times once or twice? How many times the complaints were made. And after you made the complaints did somebody monitor to you any results of anything which may have been done pursuant to those complaints against the KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through several reports we presented these complaints -- or actually, not complaints. We showed what it was that we had learned through our operative work, our intelligence work. We informed the top leaders of the state security about -- both in writing and verbally about what we had found out, and I don't know to what extent this was further conveyed to these factors who were in Kosovo. There were other people who were in charge of that. I really don't know. There were several cases of information, not only these, and it wasn't only in the territory of Pristina but throughout the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the third page in English of this exhibit, and -- that's in the English and the B/C/S I believe it is the third page as well, and the section I want to focus on is just under the discussion of the world media agencies in Albania preparing the incident relating to Racak. There is a section about: "It is NATO's official position that the guilt will be on the Serbs if they continue with the provocations in the area. KLA fighters should be careful and take more account because the Serbs are bringing the best soldiers from its central. The KLA is making a mistake when it brings the Tigers from Likovac because there is a possibility that the Serbian forces are on some other place. The Stimlje area is the weakest spot of the KLA." Could you explain for us what knowledge you have of the KLA Tigers from Likovac and any -- who were they, that is being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The service had information about what members of the KLA were doing throughout Kosovo and Metohija, particularly in that area, that's the area that we call Drenica. And if I can put that way, according to the information that we had, these were some sort of special forces of theirs that were active in that area. We provided information about that. That is where the military, the police, and the civilian population were attacked most frequently, in that area and by those units that were active in the territory of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now move to 6D202. Sir, while this is coming up in e-court I think we'll see to be an operative information from the CRDB Pristina dated the 6th of January, 1999, and again it mentions Shaun Byrnes and Bardhyl Mahmuti --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I just noticed that I have a note here that there appear to be three paragraphs in B/C/S for which we don't have a translation. They're on the -- they're the first two paragraphs at the top of the next-to-the-last page in B/C/S. It's page number 6D030906, and on the preceding page 0905, the last paragraph, it does not appear have been translated into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is your point simply that we mark it for identification or is it more substantial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I would like to have that marked for identification and then maybe I can deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. Those are not the paragraphs I was going to reference, but I agree that the translation should be complete. I will make sure that is done. For our purposes on 202 I would like to look at the last paragraph of this document, which should be on the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned -- well, first of all, the question I had started to ask was that this document references Shaun Byrnes and again Bardhyl Mahmuti. I forget if you had answered for us who Bardhyl Mahmuti was and how the RDB had information about him.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Bardhyl Mahmuti was the spokesman of the KLA for foreign countries. We received information on him because he was being directly treated by the SDB, namely that all measures -- all methods used by the service were applied in respect of him, and that is how we learned of his contact with Shaun Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the last paragraph of this document talks about the unit in Lab. Is this the information that you talked about earlier wherein Mr. Byrnes advised that they should save these forces for the so-called Kosovo spring offensive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the information, except that he said about the future not exactly about the Kosovo spring, but we knew what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the "komandant" of the KLA forces in Lab was or would have been at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Names are a bit difficult for me. Remi was his name, Commander Remi. I remember events very well, but I have a bit of difficulty with names. I know it's Remi, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could focus on the Rambouillet negotiations. Did the RDB have any kind of information regarding specifically Shaun Byrnes and his contacts with the KLA regarding Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the service received information, as I said. We were dealing with him. First of all, members of the KLA didn't want to go to Rambouillet, so it wasn't only Shaun Byrnes. Many other foreign persons were persuading them to go to Rambouillet. The second problem in relation to Rambouillet was that the leaders of other political parties, especially Ibrahim Rugova, didn't want to go with them, he didn't want to accept them as equal decision-makers and negotiators in Rambouillet. So there were problems there because these foreign representatives had quite a problem there, how they would reconcile everyone and everything. So finally what happened was they didn't even travel to Rambouillet together. They took different planes and their organizations were different in terms of going to the Rambouillet negotiations. That is one thing. Secondly, when talking to the members of the KLA, Shaun Byrnes and other representatives who helped them kept trying to persuade them that America and the rest would stand behind them at these negotiations and that they would make it possible for them to attain the objectives of their struggle in terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. We as a service found that a bit strange, very strange, what was going on there. Because in the beginning of the year, 1998 and the end of 1997, their Ambassador Gelbard had a meeting with the Kosovo representatives and he said then that the KLA was a terrorist organization, that they as political representatives of the Albanians should try to neutralize any kind of activity by the KLA. I don't know whether you have this in the evidence here, but we have this information, Ibrahim Rugova, Rexhep Qosja, Ljuljeta Pulja, Adem Demaqi, they were all present at that meeting and they were openly told that the KLA is a terrorist organization. Less than a year later, Byrnes and the rest come there and say that they are fighters for the freedom and liberation of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we at the break already or do we have more time? I think we have more time but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, is this a convenient time to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we have to have a break at this stage, Mr. Joksic. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you in an hour, that will be at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before I take up where I left off, I'd like to return to an earlier part in the testimony and I've already apologised to Mr. Hannis. He was correct that the Scorched Earth was not Mr. Surroi but, in fact, Baton Haxhiu, another OTP witness, at P2078, page 13 in the English who said that the late David Gajic told him of a plan called Scorched Earth or "Sprzena Zemlja" to expel or eradicate all Albanians from Kosovo. Sir, do you have knowledge of a plan of that nature existing within any organs of the state?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: That sort of plan certainly never existed or at least I didn't know of it when I was in the RDB. Incidentally, I do know when the conversation took place between Gajic and Baton Haxhiu and I don't believe that Gajic said that because that sort of plan never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could return to 6D201, one of the set of the documents we were looking at before the break, and if we could turn specifically to the third page in the English and in the Serbian. In the Serbian it is -- it is I believe the second paragraph and in English it is the second paragraph from the bottom; second paragraph from the top in B/C/S, second paragraph from the bottom in English. It talks about Mahmuti having a conversation with Evlianna Bajcinovci, Birane, clerk in the press office of the KVM OSCE in Pristina. Are you familiar with this individual and the contacts with various Albanian language papers and the KLA in Drenica area? Can you enlighten us about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I have difficulty reading this, but I can say generally speaking that the stations were maintaining contact with KLA representatives throughout Kosovo and Metohija. I can read this and I can't remember any specific example but I do know that they were maintaining contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any event, we do have the document. Let's move on to 6D206 -- or I take that back -- oh, yes, let's go to 6D206. You had previously orally testified about the fact that promises had been made to the Albanians relating to Rambouillet. I would like to focus your attention on this document. The second half of the second paragraph in the Serbian, should also be the second half of the -- second paragraph or just the full paragraph talking about Rambouillet. If we could zoom in on the Serbian version. It seems to be rather faint on my screen. And the last half of that paragraph talks about the discussions Mr. Byrnes was said to have with the KLA upon touring the 121st Brigade of the KLA. And if I can ask you, is that 121st Brigade of the KLA, is that unit known to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were monitoring the activities of that unit. This is the unit near Miljevci, the brigade, and that's where we obtained information indicating that Shaun Byrnes had got in touch with them and that he was promising that he would get support at the negotiations in France, support from the west. He was trying to convince them that the KLA should attend those talks as one of the political players in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we see in the second -- excuse me, the next -- the tail end of the last paragraph on that page, which in the English I believe is on the second page, the last line of the paragraph, it indicates that Byrnes enabled the KLA representatives to take their personal weapons to France to show how much he is on the side of the KLA. Is that a fact that you can confirm through the operative information that you have?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We had information showing that they had allowed them to bring weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to 6D207, another official note of the CRDB Pristina, this one dated the 29th of January, 1999, and if we could turn to the last page of this exhibit and the second-to-last paragraph of the same. Here we see some questions of Mr. Byrnes posed to Ramush Haradinaj, a KLA leader who is before this Tribunal in another matter. And he talks about inquiring whether the KVM members that met with Haradinaj in the staff of the KLA, if they passed along or told him some things. Do you have any additional knowledge to report about the RDB's information relating to meetings of the KVM with the staff of the KLA and what sorts of things they passed on to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, we had information, as this report states, about their contacts. Ramush Haradinaj was supposed to receive some information. I don't know what type of information right now. There was perhaps information involved that I can't remember, but there were contacts and he sent word through the OSCE people that the Haradinaj should be given some information. The assumption was -- is that this was probably about the imminent negotiations and they were probably advising them to hold back a little in terms of their operations so that they might be able to go to France as political representatives of the Kosovar Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the RDB have information that the KLA was preparing certain staged incidents to try and justify the commencement of NATO intervention on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: There was several situations like that. The war itself was one. This was to begin with an anti-terrorist action that was then misrepresented as an attack against civilians. There was several other examples, quite many actually. There was certain actions that were carried out by the KLA and they were wearing VJ or police uniforms. This sort of thing would be staged. A number of incidents that were then attributed to the VJ and the police. We had intelligence showing that especially during the war, I think even some foreign media talked about this, when the Kosare barracks was taken the KLA came into the possession of a large number of weapons and uniforms belonging to the VJ, and this equipment, uniforms, and weapons were later misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there going to be examples of this, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Through other witnesses, I believe. With this witness I had not intended to go through it. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it is valueless evidence, this, when we don't know what the incidents were and we don't know the extent to which there's evidence showing that they were stage managed, but if that's what you want to present from this witness, that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the RDB have information regarding any collaboration between NATO and the KLA during the course of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had a lot of information that we obtained from intercepts by intercepting satellite-link communication. We had information showing that they were directly in touch, I mean persons from Kosovo and Metohija, members of the KLA on the one hand, and NATO on the other. They were even sharing specific information about the location of certain facilities, military installations where the police and the military were, so that they might be targeted. We also had operative intelligence, this wasn't something that we could prove, but we had intelligence showing that certain locators were placed in certain buildings by members of the KLA. We also suspected during the air-strikes, we had grounds for suspicion, by analysing some buildings that were targeted, that they had been targeted with incredible accuracy. For example, General Lukic's office was hit in the SUP building and his deputy's office too. And they accurately hit the room that was three floors under the ground where meetings of the SUP collegium in Pristina would be held. In our estimate, as far as we operative officers could talk about that at all, NATO hit with incredible accuracy this room that was three floors under the ground and actually the very table at which meetings were held. This was unbelievable. And of all offices, General Lukic's office and his deputy's office were hit. We even had this creeping suspicion that the locators had been put there by representatives of the international community who had been to Kosovo on a mission beforehand. So this was a well-founded suspicion that we harboured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you find the locators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not we personally as a service. I don't know if people from the VJ or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have evidence that the army did in fact find locators at some of the locations, Your Honour, in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have that evidence of locators being discovered by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I'm interested in General Lukic's office. The suggestion -- the one example we are being given here of the KLA planting --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: KVM, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's KLA according to the transcript, and this suggestion as I understand it is a KLA member has infiltrated General Lukic's office. Now I'm interested in that and I would wonder what evidence there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We can ask for the witness to clarify. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've just asked him and he says he didn't find -- that he's not aware of them actually finding any locators, so it's a question of suspicion and no basis for this suspicion, other than that they -- a NATO weapon appears to have hit its target.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, evidence will be led from all our witnesses that every single SUP on the territory of Kosovo, the desk of the chief officer was targeted specifically, very precisely, the desk in the office of each head of the SUP, that will be brought through our many witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's hear from them in due course, but this evidence is of no value whatsoever, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to move on, sir, and ask you to tell us what you know about certain events from 1998 to 1999, for instance, could you first tell us if you know anything about the KLA attack on Orahovac town in 1998.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and there is information to that effect from the Prizren State Security Service, on the 17th of July, 1998, the KLA attacked Orahovac town with great might as well as the villages around Orahovac town. They entered the town and they even laid siege to the police station there. They blocked all the roads, they sealed off a number of roads, and this offensive of theirs went on from the 17th to the 24th of July, as far as I can remember, which was when police forces and VJ forces drove them out of that town. I do remember and I do have information showing that on that occasion 58 persons had been kidnapped or had gone missing, five of which were found dead. Women had been raped. A group comprising between 30 and 40 members of the KLA actually raped two ladies. There were those persons who were kidnapped, a total of 58, I think. Those persons were never found. Later some bodies were found in various places after the war, bodies were found. Most of the persons who were kidnapped at the time were at some point later on also killed or executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the edification of the Court, paragraph 69 of the written statement and Exhibit 6D1015 mentioned therein provide further details for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now just before I move back to that topic just to clear up one thing that I fear remains mistaken or blurred. Was the information of the DB that locators were placed by the KLA in the offices of Sreten Lukic and his deputy on the meeting room or by somebody else; and if somebody else, who?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No. When I talked about the KLA I meant that as in on the ground, some installations and facilities that were out in the field where there was combat going on and where the units were. As for the office, our suspicion at the time was that representatives of the KVM who had been to see General Lukic and his deputy actually had planted those devices. That's what we believed at the time. That was our suspicion based on this, why those offices and not some others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall ask the CLSS to give us a translation fresh of page 68 from line 9 to line 21. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we're at it, at line 20 of page 71 he mentioned the deputy of General Lukic as Mijatovic I believe, if we can perhaps avoid the necessity of CLSS having that, if I could just ask the witness whether, in fact, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, deputy, Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The women that you mentioned as having been raped, were they Albanian women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Serb women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about any parts of Kosovo, especially if any parts of major cities were not accessible to security forces in either 1998 or 1999 as a result of the KLA holding them as strongholds?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout 1998 and 1999, especially before July 1998 and later, many parts of Kosovo were under the control of the KLA, especially the Pristina-Pec road, the Pristina-Prizren road, all the roads, all the villages and towns in Drenica. As for major towns, there was certain sections of those towns where it wasn't safe, such as Pristina, for example, the Vranjevac neighbourhood in Pec, it was the Kapesnica neighbourhood; in Gnjilane it was a neighborhood of which I can't remember the name of right now but it was another neighbourhood that was extremely unsafe to move about because members of the KLA would show up wearing uniform in those parts and there was a risk that undesirable consequences might be the result of their presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you if you know of any incidents during a time-period of the KVM mission when the KLA was suspected of having killed Albanian civilians in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were many examples like that. I am going to name one. It was along a road leading from Orahovac to one of the other villages there, I can't remember the exact name. Our forces were out to sweep the ground and they found six ethnic Albanians who had been killed. Later the bodies were identified and intelligence was obtained indicating that two families had been killed. One was Berisha and the other -- well, I can't remember the names. I don't have such a good head for names, as I said before. The father of those sons who were killed, the reason that the KLA had killed him was he asked the OSCE to check the killing of one of their neighbours who was a Serb. He asked the OSCE in writing to do this. This information was probably obtained by the KLA, and those persons were found executed and their bodies were thrown into the ditch by the road. We identified their bodies and we learned about this. Two families, I think Zoga and Berisha, three persons each from these families were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the situation around the town of Malisevo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the town of Malisevo was considered to be the hotbed or where the headquarters of the KLA were, and that's -- that was their main stronghold, the greatest concentration of their forces. So all the orders to all the other units of the KLA came from there. This was a very important stronghold of the KLA, and they themselves at the time, every time they made a public address, their spokespersons always stated that Malisevo was the centre of the Republic of Kosovo where the Supreme Command of the KLA was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And can we take by that that the KLA held the town of Malisevo for a certain period of time in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. It can be considered like that. It wasn't cleansed of KLA members before the end of October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can I guess have either the intervention of the translators or have CLSS listen to the last line, I believe he said it wasn't liberated or cleared of KLA members before the end of October 1998. But that might be one that we might have to listen to to get the precise meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of weaponry did you know the KLA to possess in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, initially when the KLA were first organizing themselves and their first activities, they mostly had weapons that they had obtained of Chinese make, automatic weapons, and other small arms and weapons of Yugoslav make, the former Yugoslavia I mean. At a later stage when the KLA grew, when their strength grew, and when they started carrying out terrorist actions to a far larger extent and when there was cooperation that had been established with the players from the west, it was noticeable that they started having weapons from western countries and from NATO countries. They had some rocket-launchers and other kind of weapons that we found in their possession and that we knew to be weapons produced in NATO countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, sir, if the RDB knew of any other armed formations of Kosovo Albanian separatists that existed on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In 1998 in Metohija near the Albanian border there emerged information that had been set up by the illegal government, if I may call it that, of the so-called Republic of Kosovo by Prime Minister Bujar Bukoshi, who was living in exile in Germany at the time. These units were called FARK, armed forces of the Republic of Kosovo. For the most part the forces comprised ethnic Albanians, former JNA and policemen and people belonging to other security bodies. According to our information, our intelligence, and according to information that we obtained by questioning members of the KLA who had been arrested, the unit was between 2.000 and 3.000 strong. When they showed up in this area there was a vigorous reaction by the KLA who refused to recognise them as a force that should be involved in the fighting in Kosovo and Metohija. As a result and since this unit was actually something that had been set up by the illegal government of the Republic of Kosovo presided over by Bujar Bukoshi, in Tirana, Albania, a minister in that government, their defence minister, was killed, assassinated. I'm very bad with names. I think his last name was Kastrati, but I'm not sure. On the same day the Albanian president of a parliament, council in Albania's parliament was assassinated, the person who was in charge of defence. The reason for these assassinations, at least that's what the service learned, was that they were the ones who had set up this FARK unit, this armed formation. Therefore, both in our country and Albania the unit did not attain any high level of significance and they were soon disbanded because of efforts of the KLA. According to our intelligence, some of them joined the KLA and some of them went back to Albania or to other countries abroad where they had been living before the unit was first set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have instances or information of instances where the F-A-R-K, or FARK, entered into armed conflict or were otherwise actively opposed to the KLA in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: When they first showed up, the first reaction came from the spokesperson, Jakup Krasniqi, who said that those were no units. Over there at least according to our information there were sporadic clashes going on in Kosovo and Metohija. I couldn't name a specific example of in-fighting among their ranks, but the fact remains that this unit was soon gone and left the position that they had attained in Kosovo and Metohija also on account of the KLA increasing in terms of strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the RDB have any information about instances where ethnic Albanians were detained and/or mistreated by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, we did have information suggesting that. Many reports were written up about that. The KLA refused to recognise any of the political parties that were active or that were espousing a more pacifist solution or more pacifist policies, more peaceful policies. There was fighting on Mount Cicavica. A delegation of Albanians was on their way there to tour the theatre of war, I think Ljuljeta Pulja Beciri and the president of Kosovo's liberal party were there and they were ambushed by members of the KLA. They practically arrested them and told them that there was a list of persons to be liquidated and the list included all political representatives of Albanians who were not in favour of the KLA, who reserve their support. We gathered this information about this clash on Mount Cicavica where this delegation of Albanian politicians had arrived in order to tour that part of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe you've already testified about foreign agencies assisting in the training of the KLA. Do you have anything further you can provide in addition to what you have already said about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, we did have intelligence showing that. The KLA had already been in the process of being trained in Albania for long years, and we had intelligence showing that the Albanian security service were in charge of their training and of putting up persons from Kosovo and Metohija who would go to Albania to receive or undergo training there. At first it was Cigurimi [phoen] and then later I think the name was changed to SHIK, the SHISH of Albania, and they directly controlled all departures from Albania to Kosovo, both in terms of weapons, equipment, and persons, and they were also in charge of training because instructors of various ranks would go to Albania and members of the KLA from Kosovo and Metohija were trained there. And also members of the KLA who were living in foreign countries in the west and who would go there for training. Even prior to 1998 and 1999 our service had information about certain camps, training camps, in Germany, in Switzerland, in other countries of the west. It wasn't possible for those training camps to exist in those countries without the appropriate services of those countries being aware of it. There had been a lot of information previously showing that, I'm talking about 1995, 1996, 1997, about all these training camps that had been set up and organized in western countries. As for camps in Albania, we had a lot of information about that. The most reliable information was that concerning the way they were trained and what exactly was going on there because we had been successful in arresting or bringing in several members of the KLA who had actually undergone training in Albania; therefore, they gave us first-hand accounts of the training and how they were trained and what the focus was of that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can ask you if you could enlighten us about any of the activities in December of 1998 in the cities of Pec, Kosovo Polje, and the villages around Pristina, if you know of any KLA activity that escalated during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, over that period there were a number of -- quite a number of incidents and things going on, although it was after the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement and although this was some sort of a lull. In Pec a cafe called Panda was attacked and six or seven young persons aged between 16 and 17 were killed. Also at the time there was another incident in Pristina, or rather, in Podujevo. One of my colleagues was killed. He was the chief of the local office in Podujevo, Milic Jovic. We couldn't even have a proper burial according to our tradition because we were shelled by the KLA and we were barely able to bury the man. Likewise, at around the same time, there were incidents occurring elsewhere. I'm just giving you these two examples -- oh, yeah, right, Kosovo Polje. The vice-president of the municipality, Bojanic, was found dead several kilometres away from Kosovo Polje in a village there. Those were incidents that occurred after everything that had been happening in 1998 when people were being kidnapped, civilians specifically, for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could focus for the moment the area around Podujevo. Are you aware of any actions of the KLA regarding mixed villages around Podujevo that had a population of both ethnic Serbs and ethnic Albanians in December of 1998 and January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time members of the KLA virtually expelled all Serbs and non-Albanians from those villages. There is an incident involving the death of a Serb in one of those villages. This Serb was killed, I think his last name was Radojevic. So those villages were cleansed, they were no longer mixed-population villages. Now they were pure Albanian villages. Also in those villages around Podujevo another two Serbs, ethnic Serbs were killed who were the last persons remaining in those villages -- in that village. I think one of them was called Rakic and the other Nikolic. After that, there were no Serbs left in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the last question that I have for you is: Do you know the fate of any of your colleagues or Albanian friends or other non-Serbs that stayed on in Kosovo and Metohija after the withdrawal of Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, many of the people involved in this met a sad fate. Many of them were killed or kidnapped, and we don't know what became of them. I would like to tell you about one of our colleagues, an ethnic Albanian, Ibush Bukoshi. He worked with the service up until 1991. He was the head of the 3rd sector, which is the sector to which I was appointed when I first arrived in Kosovo. This person retired. During the air-strikes he had fled to Montenegro. When all of this was over and we had withdrawn from Kosovo and Metohija he returned to Kosovo. The first day he got there -- rather, the next day he was killed at his own door-step with his whole family witnessing this assassination. This information was provided by a colleague of ours who -- this guy was a very wonderful man, a very successful police officer. Our colleagues who had stayed behind in Kosovo and Metohija told us about this, how it happened and how he had been killed at his door-step by members of the KLA, although KFOR were already in Kosovo and Metohija at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, page 80, line 3, I think he said: Although KFOR and UNMIK were already in Kosovo. Thank you, Mr. Joksic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think one of my colleagues might have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have agreed that Mr. Petrovic will go first because we're covering the same area and I may have a question after him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Joksic, I will be asking you questions on behalf of Mr. Nikola Sainovic. I have several questions to ask you. First of all, can you please tell me at the time of the air-strikes, were you in contact with Ibrahim Rugova at any time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn Rugova's whereabouts? How did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I had received a direct order from the chief of the State Security Service sector of the RDB that we were to track down the leaders of Albanian political parties, Rugova among others, because foreign media had started publishing inaccurate information about the fact that Rugova had been killed or wounded, and the same applied to representatives of other political parties. I think this was on the 31st of March. I had been informed by the head of the Pristina centre, Misko Lakovic, that Ibrahim Rugova was staying in his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions in connection with further proceedings against Ibrahim Rugova when you learned where he was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, there was a big media campaign and speculations about whether Rugova was alive or not. When I consulted Vilotic, who was the chief coordinator, who was an assistant, as to what we should do, we agreed that we should go to Rugova's house and contact him and ask him, if he wanted to, to address the public, so that we could prove that he was alive and well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did Ibrahim Rugova address the public --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the evening around 8.30 p.m. I took the chief of the press centre in Pristina, I think his last name was Urosevic, and I went to Rugova's house with him. There I found several members of the public security in front of the house. I entered the house. I introduced myself. I said who I was. I said that I was from the state security, and I asked him whether he would like me to bring the journalists who were in the press centre in the Grand Hotel so that we could publish the news that he was alive and well, that we had found him, and if he could only make that statement to finish the matter. And he agreed. I went back to the press centre, I took all the journalists who were there, there was some foreign journalists and some of our journalists, five or six representatives of the media, and I brought them all to Ibrahim Rugova's house. And in his reception room where there were photographs where he had previously held press conferences, there was a photograph of Mother Teresa, one of his meeting with the Pope, and so on and so forth, and he stood there and he made a statement to the media saying that he was alive and well and that he was in his house in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could we just make a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can interpret everything we say. After this address to the public by Rugova, or rather, his address to foreign and domestic journalists, was there a trip or journey?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: After that press conference I -- well, I didn't order but I agreed with my colleagues from the state security that they shouldn't be inside Rugova's house, that they should be in front of his house providing security, and I brought operatives there to stand in that antechamber that I've just mentioned, the reception room, and to take care of security there, of Rugova and his family. Then I went back and I informed the chief of the state security of what had been done. This was in the course of the night, and then he called me up again, I can't remember what time it was, but it was past midnight, and he told me to go and see Mr. Rugova, the late Mr. Rugova, and asked to talk to him to ask him whether he would like me to take him to Belgrade for him to talk to the president of the FRY, Slobodan Milosevic. I carried out that order. I went to see Rugova. I told him what my chiefs were asking me to do, and I asked him whether he was willing or not to go. He said he would have to consult his chef de cabinet or maybe his chief of security Adnan Merovci. He didn't want to make a decision without him. So he went to another room, they consulted, conferred there, and on the next day they agreed to go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who did Rugova meet in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In Belgrade he met Slobodan Milosevic, the president. I think the meeting was held in Beli Dvor, and I was present during about 50 per cent of the meeting and the other 50 per cent they were alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Rugova go back to Pristina after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, after that meeting we went back to Pristina and I received instructions from the chief of the service that as of that point we, the entire service, had to take care of Ibrahim Rugova's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time on your return from Belgrade and Rugova's return from Belgrade, to the best of your knowledge, was there any contact between Nikola Sainovic and Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think so, but it's hard to recall all the details. To the best of my knowledge, on the 4th of April they called me up from the service and they said that Mr. Sainovic, the deputy prime minister of the federal government, would arrive to talk with Ibrahim Rugova, that I should provide security for this meeting. He wanted to talk to Ibrahim Rugova, and I was only told that the topic of the conversation would be for Ibrahim Rugova to agree to talk to the deputy prime minister of the Serbian government Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Sainovic arrive in Pristina at some point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, he arrived that evening. He contacted me and they spoke in Rugova's house. I took him to Rugova's house and they spoke there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know with whom Nikola Sainovic came to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Nikola Sainovic came to Pristina with an escort, and he was alone apart from that escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, in the relevant period how often did Nikola Sainovic come to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I think he came there three or four times, on three or four occasions. I took him to see Rugova, they would talk, and then he would go back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you present at those talks between Sainovic and Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: For the most part, over 70 per cent of them. I wasn't there all the time, up to the end. Those were political talks; I was not a politician, I was a professional, and sometimes I found it very boring to listen to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that Sainovic came and brought the message that a meeting should be organized with the deputy prime minister of the Serbian government, Ratko Markovic. Do you know whether Sainovic transmitted any other messages to Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, they were messages of a general political nature, that everything should be done to stop the air-strikes, to stop the war, that we should -- that the organization of government in Kosovo and Metohija should be discussed, that all displaced persons and refugees of all ethnicities who had lived in Kosovo previously should come back, and they were all, as far as I was able to tell, political issues of a general nature. And also that agreements should be made between the authorities in Belgrade and Rugova as the legitimate representative of the Albanian people, that the war should come to an end, and that a peaceful solution should be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We just mentioned Ratko Markovic. Do you know whether Rugova agreed to meet the deputy prime minister, Markovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I think he did, yes, and I think they spoke at length. The question was why Ratko Markovic, and Mr. Sainovic explained that Ratko Markovic had been the head of the delegation in Rambouillet, that he had been the head of the delegation, and in a previous period when the authorities of Serbia arrived in Kosovo he had been among the ministers assigned to discuss matters such as education. He was a constitutional expert, and so he was the best person to talk to, to find ways and means of finding a political solution to the problems in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you attended most of their talks. What was the atmosphere like at those meetings between Sainovic and Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I have to say this, there was a state of war, there were many problems, but I think that both Sainovic and the late Mr. Rugova did their best to create an atmosphere of mutual trust and confidence. That was my impression at least, and there were never any bad words or any serious conflicts. Although their viewpoints diverged initially, they always managed to smooth things out and arrive at a common goal in the end. I do apologise, I forgot to say something. The first time they went to see Milosevic, they made a joint statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but please limit yourself to my questions.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you proceed, what do you mean they managed to smooth things out and arrive at a common goal? I'd doubt if we'd be here if they had done that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regrettably, that did not happen, but Mr. Sainovic made a major effort to succeed in that. He made proposals, in fact, he conveyed the positions of the authorities from Serbia, what it is that should be done, that everything should be resolved through talks, not through war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not really my question. What did you mean by: They always managed to smooth things out and arrive at a common goal in the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they agreed that there would be political contacts and that Rugova and the political leadership of Serbia would work together for that. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: After these meetings that you described, do you know what Nikola Sainovic did afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: After contacts with Rugova and these discussions, he went to Belgrade to convey what it was that he had attained. Usually we would go late at night, he would meet with Rugova and go to Belgrade to convey what it was that they had reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Sainovic had meetings with Adnan Merovci that were not attended by Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk with Adnan Merovci too. I suggested that because I was in contact with him all the time. Our assessment was that Mr. Rugova did not want to reach any kind of agreement or make any decision without consulting Merovci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can other microphones please be switched off; we can barely hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the Sainovic-Merovci meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I think so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did at any point in time Ibrahim Rugova leave the country?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Ibrahim Rugova left the country on the 5th of May, I think, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how that happened, how come he left the country?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Before that there were quite a few activities before he left the country. On the 16th of April we were in Belgrade where Rugova had a contact with a president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, in the Presidency of Serbia. That same day he had a contact with the patriarch of Moscow, Alexei, I took him there too. After that on the 28th of April there was a contact that was followed by a joint statement in Pristina between him and the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic; Ratko Markovic, deputy prime minister was there too; then the president of the Temporary Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, Zoran Andjelkovic, was there, as well as Mr. Sainovic. That meeting took place at the building of the Executive Council in Pristina. Before these contacts took place between Mr. Rugova and the president of Serbia, the president of Serbia went to the places that had been bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you focus on the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can hardly hear the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there is some problem -- well, my microphone is one of the problems, but we are being told to put off the microphones if we can as much as possible. So when you've asked the question, Mr. Petrovic, can you put it out. It must be your microphone and mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, I've noticed, at least on my end, the shorter microphone makes less background noise than the longer microphone. That's why I switched to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Suitable for the shorter person, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I shall go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, please, how did this happen that Rugova left the country?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: That's why I told you all that I've told you already, because at this meeting with Milan Milutinovic, the president of Serbia, Milan Milutinovic, Mr. Rugova asked -- well, he said that he could not work politically from Pristina any longer, that they were outside the country, Macedonia, throughout Europe, and that it would be a good idea for him to leave the country. What was conveyed to me was, because I was not directly present there where they were having the meeting, I was in the room in front, but Mr. Rugova told me that he had asked Milutinovic and that the president had promised him to resolve that question of his within the next 24 hours. After about three days, I think, I was called from Belgrade by the chief of the service and I was told to bring Mr. Rugova and Adnan Merovci to Belgrade and that what would be organized would be their departure from the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did Rugova leave the country? Did someone come to pick him up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Since I was told to take him to Belgrade, he and I and Adnan Merovci went to Belgrade. We were in a villa, that's where we were staying. President Milosevic came there. They conducted talks there, and what was organized by the office of the head of state, Slobodan Milosevic, was that an airplane would come from Italy, it arrived on the next day, the 5th of May, at the Belgrade airport. The ambassador of the Republic of Italy in Belgrade was on that plane, and we took Rugova with his family, because in the meantime when we realized that he would be released, or rather, that he would be taken abroad, I organized two jeeps to transfer his family from Kosovo to Belgrade, and together with his family he left from Belgrade airport on the 5th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Rugova's family. From when you first established contact with him until that 5th of May, can you tell us what your relationship was like with Rugova's family, yours and your associates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that, but now I can tell you more about it. From the moment when I established contact with Rugova, and later on with Adnan Merovci, they were protected -- I know, I was made aware during the proofing for this testimony that Mr. Adnan Merovci had said that they were under house arrest. That, quite simply, was not true. We ensured whatever we possibly could through the provision of Executive Council every day milk, bread, diapers for babies, all of that was taken to Rugova's family. You couldn't buy that in Pristina in those days. That could not be bought by anyone because there was a war going on. We really made sure that everything was there. Since Merovci portrayed this in a different way, it wasn't really correct. There were two operatives in the entrance hallway, and the members of the family could freely move all about the house. The public security people were only the external security around the building. The reason why this was so was the fact that we had had intelligence that members of the KLA would liquidate Ibrahim Rugova. So we had to -- well, I had strict orders from my chief that nothing should happen to Rugova while we are taking care of him. As for the rest, well, in the beginning of the war probably because the telecommunications were damaged, their telephone was down, we, the service, managed to connect another phone for him so they were in contact with the rest of the world through that telephone with Hill in Skoplje and with other officials, whoever they wanted to contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Rugova's departure from the country. Who was there to see off Ibrahim Rugova at the airport and what was the send-off like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: When we reported that the plane was there, he was seen off from the villa with his family with several jeeps and cars. There were 17 family members of Adnan Merovci and Ibrahim Rugova. We took them to the airport. Our security was there from the sixth administration, from our service, Rugova, Merovci, the members of the family were seen off by Mr. Nikola Sainovic, deputy prime minister of the federal government; and I, and me. We made a cordial farewell. Mr. Sainovic and Rugova even embraced. I gave them a box of cigarettes and they said that they would get one back, but they never did return one, not even after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, one last question: You said that Mr. Sainovic came to Pristina several times in relation to these talks with Rugova. To the best of your knowledge, on these occasions did Sainovic present some reports to anyone or, to the best of your knowledge, did Sainovic give any instructions, orders, anything to other people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, and I think it is certain that that did not happen because he and I would always meet up and then we would go to Rugova. Many times he didn't even spend a minute longer in Pristina. As soon as he would finish talking to Rugova, he would go back to Belgrade. I was really surprised. A few times I tried to keep him there and to send him to -- to bring him to my base so that he could spend the night there. It wasn't safe to travel at night. He said, no, I have to go, I have to convey what it was that I have agreed on, so he would leave. I was worried because he'd leave. He really went through the worst area where there was the largest number of KLA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
