utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, it wasn't clear to me what your evidence was about whether there were meetings between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Merovci without Rugova being present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think there were two meetings. We talked in a building. I think it belonged to some company in Pristina. I think these talks had to do with Merovci's trip to Skoplje and after his return from Skoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, but I'm not all that sure. It has been a long time, after all. If I was not there directly, I brought Sainovic to the place where they met but I think that I attended during some parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will be very brief, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, and I am Defence counsel for General Lazarevic. I have a few very brief questions for you. You said in Kosovo and Metohija there were three centres of state security and that these centres had departments and detached offices, as they were called later. I would be interested in the following. At any point in 1998 and 1999, did any of these departments or centres or offices of the state security, was it resubordinated to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give your answer the again. The interpreter did not catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never was there any subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said "resubordination."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, I have one more question. Did you know General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to tell us what your opinion was about him and how he carried out his professional duties, if you know about that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: That is my personal opinion. I knew General Lazarevic even before the beginning of the war and we cooperated while he was -- even before he became corps commander. We saw each other in Kosovo and Metohija. I personally have a very high regard for him as a capable officer and a rather honest and good man. That was not only my opinion as that of a member of the service, but that was the opinion of most of the citizens in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joksic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Joksic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first item I want to ask you about is Exhibit P1192. I think you were shown this on direct examination, and I can give you a hard copy because it's several pages and maybe it will be easier to read, with the assistance of the usher. This is the rules of the internal organization of the RDB dated April 1996. I take it those were the rules that were in -- still in effect in 1998 and 1999, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S. I have some questions for you about article number 2. It talks about the task and the second paragraph says: "The RDB also shall carry out tasks of state administration pertaining to the security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, FRY, and prevent activities directed at undermining or toppling the Constitutional Order of the FRY." Now, the paragraph immediately preceding that said basically the same thing concerning the Republic of Serbia. My question -- my first question is: How was the RDB to operate in the situation where something might be undermining the constitutional order of the FRY but not undermining the constitutional order of the Republic of Serbia? Was that a situation that ever came to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure I understand your question. We were the RDB for the Republic of Serbia, and if there was subversive activity against Serbia then this would also amount to subversive activity against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was no Federal Ministry of the Interior at this time, was there? No Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Ministry of Interior in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There had been --

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, there was, but there was no state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did that change? Previously there had been a federal state security organ, had there -- hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, there had been until the former Yugoslavia fell apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was the top official in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia regarding tasks of the RDB? We know that there was a minister of the interior for the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Stojiljkovic; but regarding the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, who was the top official to whom RDB would answer for security tasks regarding the Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. We answered to the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. I don't think there was anyone that we answered to at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. As a practical matter in real life, didn't your ministry answer to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I can hardly say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you look at Article 3 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we'll have to go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the very top of the page it says: "The tasks of the RDB are: Counter-intelligence, intelligence, countering extremism and terrorism and other security tasks of the Republic and FRY." Now, if you'll go down to the third paragraph it says: "Intelligence tasks are the tasks of gathering, analysing, and assessing information ..." I want to skip a little bit. And it says: "... and monitoring the degree to which political, religious, and other freedoms and rights of ethnic Serbian communities outside the FRY are implemented or to which they are endangered." Now, do you know why this is limited specifically to ethnic Serbian communities outside the FRY?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, intelligence people are supposed to gather intelligence outside the country, the reason being there are Serbs all over the world. The service had the responsibility of gathering any sort of intelligence that were putting at risk Serbs, not only those living in Yugoslavia but also those living outside the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia. This is intelligence and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But it doesn't address the issue of addressing intelligence regarding threats to the political, religious, and freedoms and rights of non-Serbian Yugoslavs outside the Republic of Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: It talks about Serbian ethnic entities; that means whenever there's a rather large number of Serbs. Now, why doesn't it say the other thing, I guess you should ask someone else, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Within the RDB we see references to several different organizational units. I think this document lists up to ten different administrations within the RDB. Which administration were you a part of? Were you in the third administration? That begins at Article 13 on page 5 if you want to look at your hard copy.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was the -- that was the administration that was concerned with counteracting extremism and terrorism; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could take a quick look now at Exhibit P1228. Mr. Joksic, this is a report or a summary dated the 3rd of January, 1999, to the Ministry of the Interior. Have you seen these kind of documents before? I can --

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in. I have difficulty seeing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With the usher's help I'll hand you a hard copy of this one and that may be easier for you to follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hate to be a stickler, but this was not on the list of exhibits provided for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was on the list of exhibits I got from the Defence, and we typically advise them we are going to use any exhibits on their list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hannis be more specific, when he says "Defence," is that 6D?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, we're double-checking. It's not on our list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, on what basis are you saying that we should allow you to use it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will go to another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will go to P1224.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Joksic, let me hand you this one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document is described as a summary of the numbers of policemen in the autonomous province of Kosovo on 16 October 1998. At the bottom of the page it is dated 18 October in Pristina. And if we can go to the next page in e-court. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No -- well, I've just seen it, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't see this in 1998 shortly before the negotiations between --

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, no. This has nothing to do with the State Security Service. The numbers concerning the RJB in Kosovo and Metohija, this has nothing to do with us, that is the public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And information like that is not something that would be coming across your desk?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that you never heard of a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No. I did hear of it after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Was it 2000? 2001? There was a reference to some sort of Joint Command, but this struck me something completely new.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you happen to hear of it in 2000 or 2001? In what context?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered how he said it, he said through the press when the press started publishing this, but I'm afraid that's not in the transcript, that's page 99, line 7, so that is the answer to Mr. Hannis's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apart from anything else in the circumstances it would be a good idea to clarify it, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So please -- your question is admissible on that ground alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us, because it did not appear in the transcript earlier, in what context did you first hear about it in 2000 or 2001?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I heard several times, especially when Milosevic was taken to The Hague Tribunal and the trial began, then I heard in the press that there was some sort of an association, a Joint Command, and this purportedly existed when I was in Kosovo and Metohija as well and I had spent quite some time there and I had never heard of it, I had never heard of its existence. So that's how I heard of it. And now when I was being proofed for my testimony I was shown some documents mentioning some sort of Joint Command, but this isn't something that I'd ever heard of or personally met.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when that happened, it surprised you to hear about it, department it, because doesn't it seem to you that's something you would have been aware of, being in your position and being in Pristina in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I was surprised. I was surprised. The reason being, especially as far as 1999 was concerned. There was a war on. I spent the entire war virtually together with General Lukic, and I know there was no Joint Command nor did I ever see one. The paramount thing was to save our necks. Joint Command, no question of anything like that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, who was your boss in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: 1998? Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: David Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. And in your preparation for testifying here, were you shown the notes of meetings of the Joint Command for the period from July through October of 1998? Did anyone show you that document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Gajic never told you about all those Joint Command meetings he attended in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In 1998 it wasn't meetings of the Joint Command, it was about coordination and exchanging intelligence. For the most part this was attended by Mr. Gajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, you said you didn't know anything about a Joint Command until you heard about it in 2001. So how can you say it wasn't a Joint Command, it was a coordination body. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me, but it was like that before the war and after the war. And even ten years ago we had cooperation between the various services, the army and the public security. And depending on the situation there were meetings, monthly meetings, weekly meetings, daily meeting, it all depended on the situation that we were facing and we used these meetings to exchange information. When there were meetings like that, David Gajic would attend. I may have attended one or two myself meetings of that nature where we would submit our information, they would submit their information to us, we would exchange information, and those who decided on any further use that was to be made of this information took whatever decisions they had to take, but it was important they knew what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go slowly on this and let's just talk about 1998 first. In 1998 where were you physically located? Where was your office?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: At the state security sector building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in 1998 were you aware of the existence of a body that was called the provisional Executive Council headed by Mr. Andjelkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a Temporary Executive Council headed by Zoran Andjelkovic, a government minister in Serbia's government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we've heard it called "temporary" and sometimes called "provisional." Where were their offices located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: The Kosovo Executive Council building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was that vis-a-vis your building, how far away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: About 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know where the Pristina Corps command was located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: At about 70 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned some coordination meetings. Were these meetings that took place in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned Mr. Gajic went to some of those meetings and you yourself may have gone to a meeting or two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were those meetings held?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Depends. Sometimes the corps command, sometimes the Pristina SUP building, it really depended. I attended meetings at these two locations. I'm not sure if there were other meetings that were held elsewhere, but I wasn't there. There was a meeting I think once when Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic came, I think this was at the Pristina SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what time of day those meetings were generally held in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1998 they would be held during business hours, and later when tensions were exacerbated in Kosovo and Metohija, as far as I know, we would prepare intelligence for David Gajic, me, and his other assistants and associates, I think mostly in the evening that he went to those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a Mr. Radovic in RDB who also attended meetings in 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. He sometimes went. He was the deputy chief of the Pristina centre or deputy head. Earlier on in his career back in Belgrade he was into analysis and he wrote stuff up for Gajic, he and his team, and sometimes he would stand in for Gajic at these meetings, and they sometimes went together for the purposes of this analytical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was his first name, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Radovic, we called him Miro. Miroslav Radovic was his actual name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said earlier in the first half of 1998 that meetings would be held during business hours. Are you aware of any meetings taking place prior to July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. I can't say specifically. There were meetings that were held occasionally. Information would be exchanged. We would talk about things and reach conclusions. There were meetings at the corps command at the Pristina SUP building, public security. The only place that no meetings were held was back at our place, the state security, because we were the poorest mouse in that particular house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The meeting or meetings that you may have attended, can you tell us who you remember being present at those meetings? Can you name people for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, as for those that I attended, General Lazarevic and Pavkovic, and then from June or July 1998 onwards General Sreten Lukic or one of his staff. And we, people from the state security, those were the meetings that I went to. Before Mr. Lukic came as a staff leader I think there was another person who did the same job whose name I think was Vesovic and he was an expert in transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at none of the meetings you attended were there any civilians present, you didn't see Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Andjelkovic? None of those guys at any of the meetings you attended?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: No, not the ones that I went to, but I used to see them in Pristina because I spent a long time there and as far as I knew, they were doing their job which was politics. They were in touch with representatives of the OSCE, foreigners, many diplomats were arriving in Kosovo those days, and those were their jobs. Andjelkovic was the president of the provisional Executive Council and he would come because of what was going on in Kosovo and then Djakovic was in charge of it, they probably had to consult with him. I can't give you any details of what exactly they were doing but it was probably that, just as all the other politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 104, line 12, he was an expert in traffic, "saobracaj."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, 104 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 104, line 12, he was an expert in traffic, the Serbian word was "saobracaj."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Joksic, you don't recall Jovica Stanisic or General Djordjevic or General Stevanovic coming down and attending any of these coordination meetings?

utterances.speaker: LJUBIVOJE JOKSIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they would come to Kosovo and Metohija, but there weren't too many of those work meetings. Stanisic, when he would come, he would come straight to us, the RDB, just to see what was going on, whether we were all alive and well, how we were doing, perhaps to give us some instructions on how to proceed. As for these other generals, I think they all went there to do their own job. As for any meetings that they all had together, I can't remember a single one except when the minister came and assembled them all together, both services. There would be a meeting in order to boost our morale, to tell us to try to hold out, and then he would be off to Belgrade again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if this is going to be a suitable time to interrupt you, I have a couple of questions before we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said a short time ago, Mr. Joksic, that you spent the entire war virtually together with General Lukic, and "I know there was no Joint Command nor did I ever see one." What do you mean by "spent the entire war virtually together with General Lukic"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say was that I was there throughout. I was in charge as someone from my service in case I received anything interesting to pass this along to the staff. Incidentally, we were no longer in buildings, we were at our places and we had to find secret places where we hid in order to avoid being killed off as rabbits. We from the state security, there were two of us, myself and Rocic [as interpreted] and Lukic on the other hand had more people in his -- in his, I mean staff. So we were with Lukic at certain locations where we hid, we were together, and we couldn't have all those people in one place, it would have been dangerous, they would have been spotted. They could have picked us off like rabbits, both of them, NATO and the KLA. So we had bunkers and we had these bases that we created in an operative fashion for ourselves in order to be able to hide and that's where we spent time together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The other thing I wanted to ask you was this: Are you aware that documents with the heading and the signature "Joint Command" are evidence in the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw that as I was being proofed, but I'd never seen it before. As I was being proofed I saw some documents saying "Joint Command," which struck me as somewhat strange, but fine, not my place to judge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We now have to bring our proceedings for the day to an end, which means that you will have to return on Monday to complete your evidence. Over the weekend it is a strict requirement that you have no communication with anyone about the evidence in this case, and that applies to everyone. You can talk about whatever you like with whomever you wish, but there must absolutely no communication about the evidence. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you again here at 9.00 on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
